tr.td: Bisho (also spelled Bhisho), then the capital of the Ciskei homeland, now in the Eastern Cape, South Africa
Troops of the Ciskei Defence Force, under the military ruler Brigadier Oupa Gqozo
28 marchers and one Ciskei soldier, in most accounts

content.p: On Monday 7 September 1992, tens of thousands of people walked the last five kilometres from King William's Town towards Bisho, the capital of the Ciskei "homeland". They had come to demand the removal of Brigadier Oupa Gqozo, the soldier who ruled it. Soldiers of the Ciskei Defence Force fired on them in two long bursts of automatic fire. Twenty-eight marchers and one Ciskei soldier died, and more than 200 people were wounded. The historian Laura Evans, writing in 2024, noted that the event is understood as a pivotal moment in South Africa's transition to democracy yet has rarely been studied closely.

The killings came less than three months after the Boipatong massacre, amid tense negotiations between the African National Congress (ANC) and President F. W. de Klerk's government. The Goldstone Commission and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission later examined what happened. The first condemned the shooting and also criticised the march leaders; the second refused amnesty to two soldiers, the field commander and a rifleman.

Ciskei was one of the "independent" homelands that the apartheid state created for black South Africans. Gqozo told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) that a bloodless coup against its ruler, Lennox Sebe, took place on 4 March 1990, that the soldiers asked him to come to Bisho, and that he had not organised the coup himself. Evans writes that senior Ciskei Defence Force officers brought him to power, and that he soon turned against the ANC.

By 1992 the regime depended on Pretoria. Evans describes a government dominated by seconded South African officials in ministerial and military posts, and vigilante violence by the African Democratic Movement, which she says was backed by a South African covert military operation. The Ditsong museum, in a short history of the massacre, describes the region as the scene of a civil war driven by a repressive homeland regime and by the covert work of South Africa's security forces. That is why the march organisers addressed their demands to Pretoria. On 3 September the Border region's alliance leaders sent a memorandum to de Klerk asking for Gqozo's removal and an interim administration. South African History Online records that de Klerk rejected the request because Ciskei was outside his jurisdiction.

An earlier march on 4 August had ended without bloodshed. Riot police stopped the demonstrators at the main intersection and then let them into the stadium, according to Evans. Local leaders were determined that the next march would not be stopped there.

Almost everyone expected trouble. Gqozo had said publicly that he would stop the march. In a 14 August interview with the researcher Padraig O'Malley, quoted by Evans, he said he had told Pik Botha that he was "going to shoot the bastards if they make a false move". The day before the march, church leaders, among them Frank Chikane and Desmond Tutu, proposed cancelling it if a referendum were held to test Gqozo's support. He turned the proposal down. "We believe Monday could bring disaster," Chikane said. Nelson Mandela wrote to de Klerk on the eve of the march, saying he expected it to follow the Peace Accord and the guidelines set by the Goldstone Commission.

A strategising committee made the day's decisions. It combined Border-region leaders with national figures including Chris Hani, Ronnie Kasrils, Steve Tshwete and Raymond Suttner, and on the day it was enlarged to include Cyril Ramaphosa. In the final hours before the march a magistrate allowed the marchers to approach Bisho and assemble at the stadium. Evans argues that the permission was a formality, since the leaders never meant to stay inside it. Kasrils later said that everyone knew there was a risk, "but we believed getting rid of Gqozo was worth that risk."

The security forces were less ready than the crowd's size demanded. Evans reports that two containers of razor wire were bought to block the road, and that the wire was still being unrolled shortly before the marchers arrived. Officers ran out of it, so the stadium's existing perimeter fence had to close the rest of the line. About 1,800 Ciskei police were posted at roadblocks or sent to Mdantsane after rioting the day before, which left roughly 70 at the border. According to the Ciskei riot police chief, Brigadier Vuyisile Ngcobo, as paraphrased by Evans, he arrived on the morning of the march to find Ciskei Defence Force troops stationed around Bisho, contrary to the plan under which police would lead. Evans adds that Ciskei Defence Force chiefs had received intelligence of a planned incursion by the ANC's armed wing, and that there is evidence Oelschig was told by General van der Westhuizen, the military intelligence chief in Pretoria, to "use all means necessary" to stop the march. Oelschig asked two South African ministers that morning to halt the march, Evans writes, and they refused.

The march set off at about noon, Evans reports. At around one o'clock members of the strategising committee, Kasrils among them, went ahead to the razor wire and met two Peace Accord officials, John Hall and Antonie Gildenhuys, beside the razor wire. In Kasrils's own typescript of the exchange, submitted to the TRC, he answers a question about whether the leaders would stay in the stadium with: "Well, we're on our way, so you'll have to see." Evans reads this as showing that they did not plan to depend on the officials' mediation.

The leaders split. One group, headed by Ramaphosa, would go to the razor wire and negotiate through the peace secretariat. The other, led by Kasrils, would go into the stadium and out through a gap in its northern fence, left over from the August march, towards the centre of Bisho. The ANC's Border report, as Evans summarises it, said some marchers also forced a gap in the razor wire where it met the stadium fencing. Evans concludes that the Ciskei Defence Force deliberately watched the northern gap from hiding, with soldiers in a trench beyond it, to lure protesters through, although the Goldstone Commission disputed the ANC's claim of an ambush. A participant's assessment in the O'Malley Archive, quoting the alliance's representations to the Goldstone Commission, says that a group of about 150 unarmed people ran out of the stadium away from visible soldiers and towards a second group concealed behind trees and shrubs.

The shooting began without warning, according to those representations. Evans writes that Colonel Mkosana, believing his troops were under fire, told his commanders, who gave permission to open fire. The alliance's representations, quoted in the O'Malley assessment, describe two bursts of automatic fire: the first lasting between one and two minutes, the second about a minute. Grenades were also launched. Evans says that video evidence put the volleys at 90 and 60 seconds. She counts more than 425 rounds, while the chairman of the later amnesty panel, Judge Denzil Potgieter, said that the 36 soldiers Mkosana ordered to fire used 185 rounds from R4 rifles. The two figures are not reconciled in the sources.

Evans writes that many in Kasrils's group retreated to the stadium and were shot from behind as they ran, and that others acted as human shields for the political leaders. A police surveillance helicopter overhead led some people to believe they were being fired on from the air, she says, and the commission could not confirm that. The crowd was so dense that ambulances struggled to get through. The one Ciskei soldier who died, Rifleman Vusumzi Sydney Nqabisa, was killed by Ciskei Defence Force fire, in Evans's account.

Counts differ. South African History Online, the Ditsong museum, Evans and the TRC amnesty announcement give 28 marchers and one soldier dead. The participant's assessment in the O'Malley Archive says at least 33 died and more than 300 were wounded, with at least three paralysed, and says some people were reported missing. The TRC's July 2000 release gave more than 300 injured, while Evans, Ditsong and South African History Online say more than 200.

The question of who ordered the shooting had two answers. In September 1996 Oelschig, by then a general in South Africa's new army, told the TRC that he had radioed an "open fire" order to field commanders, according to the Ditsong museum's summary of a New York Times report. He said officers on the scene had convinced him the troops were in danger and that he told them to stop when he realised the fire "was not of a defensive nature". South African History Online, citing the TRC, says Mkosana instructed the forces to open fire and that Rifleman Gonya later fired a grenade launcher.

Gqozo told the TRC that he heard the marchers chanting and then sounds he did not at first recognise as shooting. His office issued a statement that day expressing regret at "the conduct of these marchers" and at the shooting, and conveying condolences to the families, and promised a full inquiry. He said that he had been told a soldier was shot and that fire was ordered after a report of gunfire and grenades from the crowd. He also admitted that he had signed an indemnity decree protecting his soldiers from prosecution, saying that they had acted lawfully as "the final line of defence", though in retrospect they "may have over-reacted".

The inquiry led by Judge Richard Goldstone held hearings at Bisho in late September. According to Evans, it condemned the Ciskei Defence Force's conduct "in the strongest terms" as "morally and legally indefensible". It also sharply criticised the march leaders. Their decision "to risk the lives of their followers" by advancing out of the stadium was, in the commission's words, unfortunate and unjustified, and it was "irresponsible and deliberately placed such people in imminent danger which resulted in death and injury". The commission called Kasrils's failure to tell the Peace Secretariat of the plan "disingenuous", and urged the ANC to censure him. It disputed the ANC's claim that the hole in the fence was a trap.

The Ciskei government argued before the commission that the crowd was armed. It cited press reports, including one in which Hani told a comrade holding a gun to "put it away, Comrade" because he would cause a massacre. Evans writes that some regional leaders knew vehicles carrying ammunition had been arranged to accompany the march. She also judges that the ANC's own Border report, by showing how determined the crowd was to reach Bisho, lent weight to the soldiers' claim that they fired in self-defence.

On the morning after the massacre Mandela joined a memorial march from King William's Town, where Tutu told the survivors that no lie would prevail for ever. Mandela argued that "bigger forces" stood behind Gqozo. De Klerk blamed the ANC's mass action campaign, and Gqozo also blamed the ANC. A mass funeral for the first victims followed on 18 September, which the participant's account says drew over 100,000 people.

The deadlock in national talks was broken in the weeks that followed. Mandela and de Klerk signed a Record of Understanding on 26 September 1992, in which the National Party acknowledged the right to public demonstrations in line with the National Peace Accord. Evans reports that the ANC called off mass action on 30 September; United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali had urged it to abandon the campaign. South African History Online says the Record paved the way for the resumption of formal negotiations in 1993.

The TRC held hearings on Bisho in September and November 1996. Gqozo gave evidence in November. He told the survivors in the hall that he did not know them, said he regretted that it had ever happened, and asked them: "please forgive me". He added that he did not deserve their forgiveness. A commissioner said the apology would be hollow unless it came with the whole truth. Evans reports a claim by Colonel Silence Pita of the Ciskei Defence Force that a security report reached Gqozo on the day of the march, warning of a coup plan by the ANC's armed wing.

Two soldiers applied for amnesty. At a hearing in King William's Town, in February 2000, Mkosana said he gave the order after being fired on. Gonya, who admitted firing two grenades, said the troops were told to fire three times and that nobody fired at the soldiers. Lawyers for the ANC and the victims said both men had not made full disclosure. Judge Potgieter said that 185 rounds could not be described as minimum force.

On 10 July 2000 the Amnesty Committee refused both applications. It held that their acts were not associated with a political objective, and that some marchers had broken the permit conditions by rushing towards the stadium. But "to simply open fire on everyone under the pretext of enforcing the conditions of the permit was totally unjustified", Potgieter said. The committee called the troops' conduct reckless, said a warning would probably have sent the breakaway group back, and rejected Gonya's evidence that he used the launcher on orders from Mkosana, which Mkosana denied.

A monument was put up at the site in 1997, South African History Online says. On 7 September 2025, thirty-three years on, the Eastern Cape government and the victims' families were to mark the anniversary at the memorial site at the Bhisho stadium, with a wreath-laying followed by a social dialogue, SABC News reported that day. Evans argues that the ANC's later account of the day was carefully shaped to legitimise its leaders and its national strategy, and she doubts the leadership's claim that the decision to leave the stadium was unanimous.
